summary: Provides information about the policy statements submitted by the UNINETT Policy Certification Authority. It records how that authority operates in the certificate hierarchy. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The rules a trusted ID-card office follows when it hands out proofs of identity.

subtitle: Operating rules for a Norwegian certificate authority

tldr.problem: Organizations need a trusted authority to issue digital certificates that prove identity, but the authority must operate securely and follow clear policies to remain trustworthy.
tldr.mechanism: UNINETT, Norway's academic network operator, established a Policy Certification Authority (PCA) that certifies lower-level authorities (CAs and RAs) within the hierarchy, with specific security requirements, naming conventions, and operational procedures.
tldr.outcome: This RFC documents UNINETT PCA's operating policies so organizations can decide whether to trust certificates issued under UNINETT's authority.

today: RFC 1875 is an Informational RFC documenting UNINETT PCA's policies as they existed from 1995 to 1998. It has not been updated or obsoleted and remains a reference for understanding how UNINETT operated its certification authority during that period.

sections.title: UNINETT and Its Certificate Authority
sections.content:
UNINETT is a limited company operating Norway's academic and research network. The UNINETT Policy Certification Authority (PCA) is a trusted authority that issues certificates proving the identity of other certificate authorities and users. This RFC documents the policies that govern how the UNINETT PCA operates.

The policies address how certificates are issued, how they are managed, what security measures protect the PCA, and what procedures organizations must follow to participate. The document is intended for organizations considering whether to trust a certificate that traces back through UNINETT's authority.
sections.plainLanguage: UNINETT runs a trusted office that hands out digital identity cards. This explains all the rules the office follows to make sure the cards are real and trustworthy.

sections.title: The Certification Hierarchy
sections.content:
The UNINETT PCA manages a three-level certification tree: the PCA itself at the top, Certification Authorities (CAs) in the middle, and users or Registration Authorities (RAs) at the bottom. There is typically one CA per UNINETT member organization, and it may either be run by the organization itself or by the organization operating the PCA.

Registration Authorities are designated people who perform local identity verification on behalf of a CA. Because they must physically verify identity before forwarding certification requests, they are not permitted to issue certificates themselves. Instead, an RA forwards a properly authenticated request to the CA, which issues the certificate. This separation of duties strengthens security: a stolen RA credential does not allow certificate issuance.
sections.plainLanguage: The UNINETT office sits at the top. Below it are local ID-checking offices run by organizations. Below those are trusted people at each organization who check that applicants are really who they claim to be, then report back to their local office.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
The PCA enforces strict security measures to protect its private key. The PCA's key is stored on a smartcard and the PCA runs on a dedicated workstation with no network connection. All data exchange uses magnetic tapes or floppy disks rather than networked communication. The PCA RSA key pair is 1024 bits long, and backups are stored in at least one off-site location under physical security.

CAs must meet similar requirements: a dedicated, network-disconnected workstation, secure physical protection, and a minimum 1024-bit RSA key pair. RAs, which are individual people rather than systems, must use workstations with remote login disabled and at least a 512-bit RSA key pair. The RFC states that detailed security requirements documents are made available online and must be followed by all participants.
sections.plainLanguage: The main office keeps its secret key in a safe, locked away from the Internet, with copies stored in another building. Local offices do the same. People who check identities must use secure computers without remote access.

sections.title: Certification and Naming Procedures
sections.content:
To be certified, a CA must sign a legal agreement with the UNINETT PCA. The PCA evaluates whether the people running the CA have the necessary qualifications and resources to operate it securely, and the CA must submit a self-signed certificate. RAs follow similar procedures with their certifying CA.

Users can be certified individually or in bulk. Individual certification has the user generate their own key pair and send a self-signed certificate request to an RA, who verifies identity in person. Bulk certification is used when certifying many users at once (such as students at semester start); the CA generates keys and certificates, encrypts them with DES, and delivers them via email with the decryption password collected in person or sent by certified mail.

User and RA certificates have a maximum 2-year validity period, while CA certificates may be issued for up to 10 years. DNs (Distinguished Names) follow naming conventions to ensure uniqueness, using the organization name and personal name. Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) must be issued at least once monthly and published via X.500 or mail responder.
sections.plainLanguage: Local ID offices apply to the main office to get certified. People can get their ID cards one at a time, or an office can generate many at once and hand them out. All cards expire after a certain time and need renewal.

sections.title: Policy Validity and Software
sections.content:
These policies are valid from October 1, 1995 through January 1, 1998. Information about the UNINETT PCA is available at its web site.

The software needed by CAs, RAs, and users is based on the SecuDE package from GMD Darmstadt and is available without charge for non-commercial purposes. All software distributions are signed by the UNINETT PCA to verify integrity, and users are expected to verify these signatures immediately after installation.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules were set for a specific period of time. The office provides free software to help people use the system, and all software is digitally signed to prove it is genuine.
